speechtext:
I am not like the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean)-I have no advice to give the Prime Minister. But I wish to say, that if the bill of fare is very small, possibly there is a reason for it. 1 remember reading a speech made by the Prime Minister at the Industrial exhibition at Toronto. If he is rightly reported, the right lion, gentleman stated that he himself had become a Conservative. I am not exactly certain whether that is so or not. He further said that he did not consider that a great deal of reform is now necessary in this country, the reforms that were necessary having been brought about. If that be so, the present government have accomplished wonders, in five or six years, because when they sat on this side of the House, everything was wrong. I am about as well pleased if the Prime Minister did turn Conservative. I know from experience that, as people grow older they grow more Conservative in their ideas. Some of you Radicals well know that if you had been able to carry out the ideas you had in your youth, dire calamity would have followed. So I can well understand that the Prime Minister could see that, if he had carried out some of his ideas it would have been a sorry thing for Canada. But when' the right hon. gentleman says that there is little more to reform, I take issue with him. I know well that when the members of the government sat on this side of the House, they agitated for reforms that have not been carried out-and, what is more, they have made no attempt to carry them out. Why, according to these hon. gentlemen the Senate was in such terrible state that it needed reforming, if not abolishment. But now we find that some of the men who pronounced the Senate a set of old grannies of no earthly use are breaking their necks, almost, to secure appointment as members

of the Senate. Then, we know that taxation in this country is not what it ought to be. We know that a comparatively poor man, for instance, a farmer or a labouring man with a large family, must buy a considerable quantity of dutiable goods and so may be compelled to contribute more to the revenue than many another man who is a millionaire. Some steps should be taken by this government who profess to be reformers to mend this matter. Aud it seems to me that it would be easy to do it.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: How ?

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
I am satisfied that there is not a gentleman in this House but has been properly brought up; and any gentleman who has been properly brought up will keep quiet till I am through. I do not intend to discuss the amendment before the House, because, if 1 did, I might do as some of those who have discussed it this afternoon have done, even the mover-I might wander all over creation and finish up in the Georgian Bay canal. Referring to the first paragraph of the speech, the government may well be thankful to Providence for the bounties showered upon the country. I suppose the government will hardly claim credit for the great crop in the North-west, if they do, they might as well take the responsibility for the Chinch bug, the Hessian fly and the failure of the pollen of the apple trees to be so distributed as to assure a crop. We are all thankful to Providence, but, so far as the Speech from the Throne is concerned, the government might as well have left that paragraph out. What the government should do is to stimulate every man to industry, for it is the industrious man, the tiller of the soil, the man at the anvil and other toilers who build up a country-not the government. Governments can do but little. Of course, they can make some men rich, as they are doing; and they can make a great many of us poor by over taxation and by not distributing taxation in the proper way. However, I suppose we shall be able to discuss that subject during the Budget debate. The next paragraph is in regard to the visit of the present Prince aud Princess of Wales, then the Duke and Duchess of York. I had the honour to ask the Prime Minister last spring if a programme would be prepared so that we working people might know where to meet our Royal visitors. We met them at different points of the Dominion, and I was proud to see the grand reception accorded them by the people, a reception that will redound to our credit throughout the British Empire, as their visit will assist us in many ways, and not least by helping to build up the country and add to its wealth. The next paragraph tells us of the assassination of
President Lincolu

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
Well, we always allow an Irishman to speak twice. Unfortunately for me in this case I am not an Irishman. I have had the pleasure of shaking hands with Mr. McKinley ; perhaps some of you who have had that honour did not confer any credit on Mr. McKinley. However, that was just a slip of the tongue-you all know who I mean. Now there is not a person in the Dominion of Canada who did not deplore that act. I am sure that anything this government could do, anything the people of Canada could do, to prevent anything like that occurring again, they would be only too pleased to do it. I think, perhaps, it will not only be a warning to us but it will be a warning to all civilized people to look more closely after men who are disposed to do such things.
The next paragraph, I see, deals with the census. Now I am sorry there are not some other members of the Cabinet in their seats because I would like to speak about them.
I don't think the country will believe some of the bachelors in the Cabinet when they complain so much that Canada is not more populous than it is. There are some others besides bachelors in the Cabinet and in the House too, who perhaps don't like that very well. At the same time I think one good, first class, home-bred well bred Canadian, is worth half a dozen Doukliobors or Galicians. I think there are people who are not discharging their duty to the country as they should, they are not doing wliat they ought for this Canada of ours. Now that may be a subject some of you do not approve of, but it is the basis of our prosperity ; if not, why do we wail so much at tlie poor showing of our census ?
The next paragraph is in regard to Mr. Marconi. It is not necessary for me to say anything about the great Italian who is about to send messages through the air and talk between Great Britain and Canada without any wires. I think the government was justified in encouraging Mr. Marconi and every other man of talents and abilities to come to Canada. Therefore I think the government is justified in doing their utmost in giving him encouragement.
Tlie next paragraph is in regard to exhibitions. I am sorry tlie Minister of Agriculture is not in his place. But I can talk to him another day. The Minister of Agriculture and I ought to be particular friends, because we are working at the same job. I did not have the pleasure of visiting the Glasgow exhibition, nor the Paris exhibition : but I had the pleasure of going to the Pan-American on two occasions. I was very much pleased with the exhibit Canada made there ; in fact in every department in which this country took part, she did so with credit to herself. I was much pleased with the Canadian exhibit, in fact every exhibit sent from the Dominion was a credit to us. I had the honour of speaking



.[DOT]it that exhibition before 3,000 people, and you may be sure that I held up the Canadian end of Ihe argument, and a number of Americans there who were quite qualified to judge of these matters said they had no idea that Canada could produce any such thing. One gentleman on the grounds told me that he wondered how it was I had come all the way from Canada to the Pan-American, and I told him that I could almost throw a stone from there into our country. He seemed quite surprised. So you see 1 was not the only ignoramus who was there. I told them that I would never suspect 1 had not a Canadian audience before me when I saw the well dressed people and their good behaviour I was pretty sure that I had a Canadian audience before me. But when I told them that in Ontario, in Upper Canada, as it was then, when the first legislature met within 30 miles of where we were standing, the first law that was placed on the statute-book by that legislature was that no man should be permitted to own another man, then I got no cheers there, nor here either. But they did not see the point, and you do not. It took them a hundred years to reach the point that our forefathers reached at Newark. So you see Canada has always been in the vanguard of civilization, of liberty, of freedom and pf justice. Now. Sir, I think that is enough. I could go on and tell you of many other things I said that might redound to my credit at that Pan-American, but I think that is enough.
Next, in regard to the revenue of this country. I am sure that every man on this side of the House and on the other side are only too pleased to learn that this country is prosperous. When the revenue is not raised from the proper sources then we have a right to complain. It is easy enough for this government to raise a revenue if they please, if they put the taxes high enough they can raise a high revenue. But the people of this country should not be taxed to death. The goveimment should be economical in the management of this country, and take the taxes off the people as much as possible. So we need not boast so much about revenue, because it is easy for this government to raise a revenue. If I was Prime Minister of this country and had a large following at my back, if I had a large brute majority behind me, I could do as I pleased. I could get the revenue from whatever source I pleased. What I want is that the revenue shall be derived from the proper source. The next subject dealt with in the Speech from the Throne is the increase of market facilities. I am sure that on both sides of the House we are only too pleased to learn that we have established markets all over the civilized world where Canadian products are used. What we want is an open market. There is one little kingdom that is always ready to grant us an open market for everything we Mr. ROBINSON (West Elgin).
produce in Canada ; yet some lion, gentleman over here do not appreciate it. If I were asked to give the government advice like my hon. friend for East York (Mr. Maclean) I would give it different advice from that which the hon. gentleman gives it. I should ask the Prime Minister to take 40 per cent off the tariff on English goods instead of the 334 per cent now allowed. I should also ask him to endeavour to have the embargo removed from our cattle. That is about the only embargo that we now have against our exports to Great Britain. I think that the proposition to send fast vessels to Europe and to Great Britain, if carried out, will be of very great assistance to us and I take issue with some of those hon. gentlemen who have argued here today that it would be an injury to Canada to have a fast steamship line runinng to the Cape. I feel confident that the Cape of Good Hope, and in fact the whole of South Africa, will some day be as we are in Canada, under one flag and one government, and when that result is achieved I am sure a great trade will be established between Canada and that country. I hope, in fact, I feel pretty sure, that there is spirit and enterprise and adventure enough in our young Canadian men to seek homes in that sunny clime, and wherever our Canadian boys go they are almost sure to be a credit to us. I think if a large number wept to South Africa it would be well for us. We can raise more boys and import more. Let our young men go to the gold fields and become rich as some of them have already done.
The next subject which I find, and I have to take them up seriatim, is the invitation of the right hon. gentleman to attend the coronation. I would like to be a minister for a while. I had the honour myself of being present at the Queen's jubilee in 1887 and I would like to go to the King's Coronation in 1902. I do not expect I shall be able to have sufficient means to enable me to go. It will be one of the grandest jubilations that ever took place in Great Britain and I am sure that the representative of Canada will do justice to our country. I am sure the right hon. Prime Minister will bring the questions to be discussed at the conference to be held in London before the great men from the colonies in an able manner, and I feel confident that our representative will be no disgrace to Canada. The right lion, gentleman lias represented us upon a former occasion. The Prime Minister was sent to Great Britain in 1897 by this goveln-ment and we all know-since he is not here 1 may say a little more about him than I otherwise would-that his sunny ways won the favour of all parties in England. He was placed in the front rank of the procession and we know that he did great credit to us. I would not care if he had been the biggest Tory under heaven, if he had done as well ns he did. He is a Frenchman and

he showed to the world that he represented 2,000,000 Frenchmen living under the British flag and that they enjoyed that glorious freedom and liberty which is dealt out to all classes of the people, high and low, rich and poor, of whatever nationality, creed or colour, showing that all are welcome in this Dominion and in the British Empire, if they behave themselves. I was pleased to know that the right lion, gentleman was enabled to show to the people of Europe that a statesman of French origin could speak in such terms of that glorious flag which has made the whole world bow in obedience to it. I hope that the Prime Minister, when he goes to England this summer, will be able to speak in similar terms of the flag and the institutions under which we live and hope that the men who go there to back him up will be no disgrace to him or us. We heard a good deal of discussion this afternoon in regard to the railway question, but I do not think it would be proper for me to take part in that discussion because it was irrelevant to the question. I agree with the idea expressed by the hon. member for Dabelle (Mr. Bourassa) that the government should take some steps to bring about an improvement in the management of the railways in Canada. I do not remember exactly the words which were used by the hon. gentleman, but what I would do is this : 1 would advise the government, and I see there is one member of the government present, and he can teil the rest-I would tell the government-

I would tell them, and I want them to take this matter introduced by the hon. member for Dabelle, into their serious consideration, that they should appoint, at this session, twenty-five of the brainiest men on both sides of this House to meet together in solemn conclave and take up this question of railways, their ownership and management, and consider how railways can be best managed for the good of the people of this country. I would like to have a committee appointed of not less than twenty-five of the best men. They are not all in the cabinet. Now, gentlemen, I am afraid you laugh, but I mean what I say.

speechtext: Well, I have mentioned the word ' Speaker ' half a dozen times to-night. If I have not done it sufficiently, I apologize. Now, I think I have exhausted the subject. I have spoken half an hour and that is as long as I usually speak. I thank the House very much for the courtesy it has extended to me and I hope I will not bore the House much more this session.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: Air. Speaker, just for a few moments I wish to take up the time of the House in discussing the amendment made by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) and also to ask the attention of the House to the serious condition of affairs that now faces Canada in connection with the question raised by that hon. gentleman. We had, this afternoon, a deliverance from the hon. Alinister of Public Works (Air. Tarte) and what he said to the House I do not quite know. He did not speak for himself; perhaps he spoke for the constraint in which he is at present by reason of his association with the government. I believe that if the Alinister of Public Works could express his own mind he would express a fear of the present situation. I believe he would express a fear of our railways passing into the hands of American corporations, and that he would if he could stir up his colleagues in order to save the situation. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Tarte) took occasion this afternoon to bring forward the French river navigation project, and he brought it forward in such a way that he did not. endorse it, nor did he say that the government was committed to it. Why he submitted the scheme to us I cannot quite tell. His argument was, that if our railroads are to be taken over by the Americans. then we have the system of canal navigation to fall back upon.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: And the canal is not built.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
The canal is not built. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Air. Tarte) did not answer the issue raised by the hon. gentleman from Labelle (Air. Bourassa), but, on the contrary, he evaded it. He gave the House no information, and he is not here to-night to give the House information. In reference to the Canada Atlantic Railway, the minister argued that the railways are no necessary part of the transportation system. He held that our whole dependence was on the canals, and then he launched his French river scheme. 1 was reminded of something that took place in this House last session, and, in all seriousness, I want to direct the attention of the House to that incident. There was a document circulated in this House, addressed to the Prime Alinister and to the Governor in Council, and the sum

115
and substance of it was that the members ot the House of Commons, having in view the solution of the transportation problem, petitioned the Governor in Council, and petitioned the Prime Minister, to commit the credit of Canada for $65,000,000, to be placed in the hands of a private corporation for the construction of the French river and the Ottawa ship canals. I would like that the members of this House who signed this document should stand up here to-night and justify it. And yet when that document was in my hands it was signed by 80 per cent of the members. There was another statement in that document to the effect that the signers would not regard the question as a political one. Well, sir, no member of this House cau commit me to any such statement. No member of this House can commit me to the principle of giving $65,000,000 of the people's money to a private corporation. The administration that gives this money must take the responsibility for doing so, and those who sit opposite the administration are bound to oppose it. I challenge any of the men who signed that document to stand up here and to declare that they have committed me or committed the Conservative party to any such policy as that. I believe that the Minister of Public Works was in league with it. 1 believe he was willing to pledge tile credit of this country to the tune of $65,000,000, to be given to a private corporation which was to own and to control the navigation of the French river and the Ottawa river. I regret to say that three-fourtlis of the members on the other side of the House and three-fourths of the members on this side signed that document, and I call on the Prime Minister now, and I call on the Minister of Public Works, to produce the document and let us know what the meaning of it is.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: Move for a return.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
I will move later on for the production of that document. The Minister of Public .Works this afternoon relied on that canal project for the solution of the transportation problem, and he has been a party to the circulation of that document in the House. If that be so, what is the significance of his proposition that we should rely on the canals to solve the transportation question. The minister told us that the Canada Atlantic Railway was not an essential part of the transportation system. I call on the members from the maritime provinces to consider that. This government committed itself to the extension of the Intercolonial Railway from Quebec to Montreal, and that was done in view of solving the transportation question. If they were justified, as they claimed, in extending the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal. they were justified in extending that system to the great lakes. They cannot justify their deal with the Grand Trunk Mr. MACLEAN.
Railway if it did not mean to put the Intercolonial Railway in touch with the great lakes and in touch with the traffic of the great west. If the maritime members have confidence in the government railway, if they have confidence in its extension to Montreal, they are the men who should stand up here to-night and urge upon the government the extension of the road to the Georgian Bay.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: What did it cost to bring it to Montreal V

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: I cannot give the cost at the moment, but I do say that the Intercolonial Railway is only at the beginning of traffic when it stops at Montreal. Its terminus ought to be on the Georgian Bay, and I go further and say that its terminus should be at the Niagara river and the Detroit river.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: What would that cost ?

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
No matter what it would cost. If it proves to be the true solution of the transportation problem it will cost little compared with the advantages it will afford. If the government were in earnest, and if they were up to date, they would solve the question. It is not the money you put in the railways that counts; it is the traffic tolls that carry on the railways, and the people pay them. As I said last session, I repeat now : the government can take over the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway on an agreement to pay $1 a year rental and assume the liabilities. There is no great financial proposition involved, because, as I have said, it is the traffic that carries on the railroads, aud not the people who put the capital in them. I do not agree with the Minister of Public Works that our canal system is the sole hope of the country. I say that the railroads are the complements of the canals, and if you are going to solve the transportation problem and are in earnest about it, you must take over the railways as well as the canals. The two go together. In view of the competition in the United States, in view of the acquisitive character of the people of that country, in view of the way in which the railway corporations of the United States fire grabbing our railroads, there is no solution of the problem, there is no hope for a Canadian nationality, unless the people of Canada control the railways as well as the canals. Some gentlemen may say that there is nothing much in this contention, just as the Prime Minister says he is not afraid of the situation. But my opinion, supported by that of a great many experienced men, is that we must own the railways as well as the canals, and that if we are true to our country, we ought to have courage to take both under our control. If we had the courage to do what France and

other nations have 'lone, what would he the result? What would happen to-day if the whole Canadian transportation system was taken over by the state and put into the hands or an administrator like Mr. Hays of the Grand Trunk Railway. In the first place, the whole system would be run at a much less cost, and we would have ten times the efficiency.
Once the state took over all these single track roads, they would be immediately converted into double-track, treble-track or quadruple-track systems. That means a great deal in the organization and efficiency of a railway and in the way of reduction of the cost of maintenance. One man or one body could administer the whole Canadian system of railways at one-half the cost at which it is administered now, with ten times the efficiency and at one-fourth the rates that now prevail. There is no other way of solving this problem. Of course, the plan is to bring forward one navigation scheme or one railroad scheme after another and have them bonused by this House; and we are told that this scheme or that scheme is going to save the country. But not one of them lias done it yet, nor will it be done until the two systems of rail and water communication are bound together, and the Canadian people have the courage to own and control them for themselves. The Prime Minister to-day applauded the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals when he said that Canadians had no grievances against the railways running across Canada to-day. Haven't we ? Where is the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. MacLaren) ? The other day the hon. gentleman, in addressing the dairy interests of Ontario, showed that the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway were charging more for carrying the dairy products of Ontario than they charge for carrying the dairy products of the western states through Canada. There is a grievance. The ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart), says the government ought to correct it if it is wrong, and the Premier echoed his remark. But they are not doing it, and these railroads which we have subsidized so largely are actually discriminating against Canadians and against Canadian ports. The great Grand Trunk, to which we have given so much money, is building up Portland, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have told us that they will go to Boston if they are not given certain terms. If that is the condition ol' affairs in tills country, it is high time that the Canadian people rose to the situation and took over these railroads and administered them in the interest of Canada. Mr. Speaker, it must come to that, and I thought the lion. Minister of Public Works, when he spoke this afternoon, would go in that direction; but he chose simply to bring forward another scheme entailing a great
expenditure of some $05,000,000, as a means of saving the country in regard to transportation.
Now, I am here to protest against any more expenditure on behalf of private corporations in connection with the transportation problem, and I want some member of the government this evening to answer me in regard to the proposal to commit the credit of this country to the expenditure of $05,000,000 to enable a private corporation to take over the Ottawa and Georgian Bay Ship canal project. The question must be answered. When I saw that document at the close of last session I tried to get an answer. I was too late then ; but we must have the answer now when the Minister of Public Works comes forward and tells us that the salvation of the country lies in this proposition-and I believe that he is in league witli a private corporation to take over that proposition.
This Canada Atlantic Railway, of which we have heard so much to-night, would have been a first-class investment for this country to have taken over and made a portion of the Intercolonial. The Prime Minister says that it could not be done; the Minister of Public Works says that it could not be done. Why could it not be done V If they could take over certain little railways in the province of Quebec and bind them together and make them a portion of the Intercolonial, why could they not take over the Canada Atlantic ? I believe they did desire to take it over, but they were too late. If it were taken over and made a part of the Intercolonial system, you would have a continuous system from the great lakes to the seaboard, owned and controlled by the Canadian people, and it would be a constant check on the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway. If you had the Intercolonial extended to the Georgian Bay, which could be done at a cost of $10,000,000, on which 3 per cent amounts to only $300,000 a year, what would happen ? You would have the eastern end of a transcontinental system which would be competitive with the Canadian Pacific Railway. You would be in touch with Port Arthur, from which point you would meet the Mann & Mackenzie system opening to the west; and there is a great canal sytem projected from Port Arthur to the west which may be opened one of these days. Therefore it would be good national policy for the government to have taken over the Canada Atlantic Railway.
So I make the charge to-night that the Minister of Public Works, in bringing forward the scheme which he has proposed for the salvation of the country, is bringing forward the scheme of a private corporation, and not the scheme of the country. I also make the charge that if the government were honest in extending the Intercolonial from Quebec to Montreal,

they were in duty bound to extend it from Montreal to the Georgian Bay; because, I say it in all seriousness, there is no solution of the transportation problem but public ownership of the canals and public ownership of the railways, and putting an end to this giving of the credit of the country in order to grant immense bonuses to private corporations. There is no other way out. It is all very fine to bring forward the old ideas of the last century to settle these new questions of the twentieth century. They will not do. There are a new class of men and great new forces in the world to-day. Men are quicker, men are greater, public questions are wider, and they must be approached on new lines and by new methods. Do you know what is at the bottom of that Georgian Bay Ship Canal proposition? Let me tell you. The greatest water powers in Canada which have not passed into the hands of private corporations are, along the line of the French river and the Ottawa ' river, and the scheme is to bag all these water powers in connection with this canal proposition. It is nothing but a great exploitation scheme that might figure very largely in the next general election. I had almost expected that it would figure in the Ontario elections about to come off. For my part I take this occasion to repudiate that document, which I had in my hand,'in my place, near the close of last session, and which, I believe has been presented to the Governor General in Council and the Prime Minister. And I ask the Minister of Public Works now whether, after the speech he made this afternoon, he will bring that document down, alleged to have been signed by members of this House, and explain lxow he can make the proposition he did in favour of the government constructing the French River canal if three-fourths of his supporters and a great many members on this side are committed to a proposition to give the credit of this country to the raising of $65,000,000 by a private corporation.

speechtext: I have heard the suggestion made by my hon. colleague the Minister of Public Works to my hon. friend from Labelle regarding the withdrawal of his amendment, and I would ask my hon. friend whether he desires now to press the amendment or whether he will withdraw it.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: As I have already said, I have not brought this up as a motion <Jf want of confidence or with the view of asking the government to commit itself to any policy whatever. But I consider the matter one of great importance, to which the attention of the government ought to be at once directed, in order that they may take occasion to study the question and come to a conclusion as soon as possible. If the government would announce its readiness to give the question its most serious considera-

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: tion and come to a decision before the session is over, I am ready to withdraw the motion.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: I think I can relieve my hon. friend's mind with regard to our studying the question, for I do believe that the government have already given it serious study and consideration. Whatever difference there may be between the hon. gentleman and others regarding the motion lie has presented, we all recognize that the transportation problem is a matter of the geatest importance to Canada. The difficulty with the hon. gentleman's motion is that it does not lead to anything in particular. It merely asserts that this is an important question, and if this were stated in any other form, we could all sympathize with the hon. gentleman and agree in the statement. However, he will have ample opportunity to bring up the question again, and he will lose nothing whatever by allowing it to rest for the present and withdrawing his motion. I can assure him that there is no disposition on the part of the government to do otherwise than assist in bringing the question before the House in an intelligible and useful form and in coming to a conclusion most satisfactory to the general interests of the country.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
After the explanation of the hon. minister, I am quite ready to withdraw the motion with the consent of the seconder.

speechtext:
The MINISTER OF FINANCE delivered a message from His Excellency the Governor General.

Mr. SPEAKER read the message as follows :-

The Governor General transmits to the House of Commons estimates of sums required for the service of the Dominion for the year ending June 30, 1903, and in accordance with the provisions of the British North America Act, 1867, the Governor General recommends these estimates to the House of Commons.
Government House,
Ottawa, February 17, 1902.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved that the message of His Excellency and the estimates be referred to the Committee of Supply.
Motion agreed to.
